**[p. 344]** **Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ** (The Chapter of Sincerity)

It is also called *al-Asās* (The Foundation) and *al-Muqashqisha* (The Purifier), and *Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad* (Say: He is Allah, the One).

Its central purpose is to make clear the reality of the Most Holy Essence by showing that He is exclusively characterised by the utmost perfection, so as to indicate the correct belief in sincerity (*ikhlāṣ*) in monotheism (*tawḥīd*). This is done by affirming perfection and negating every trace of deficiency and defect, which yields good speech and action and steadfast reliance and dependence in all circumstances. The name *al-Ikhlāṣ*, which brings about deliverance (*khalāṣ*), indicates this, and so do *al-Asās* and *al-Muqashqisha*. In the *Qāmūs* it is said: "*al-Muqashqishatān* are *al-Kāfirūn* and *al-Ikhlāṣ*," meaning they absolve (their reciter) of hypocrisy and polytheism, just as *al-hanā'* (tar) cleanses the mange. *Al-hanā'* is tar. The Imam ʿAbd al-Ḥaqq said in his book *al-Wāʿī*: "As the medicine cures the patient of his illness when he is cured of it" – end of quote. The word is derived from *al-qashsh*, meaning gathering, and the two chapters were so named because they follow us (in removing) hypocrisy in all its forms, and likewise polytheism and disbelief; they gather these and negate them from their reciter, if he recites them as they should be recited. The discussion of this name has already been treated at length in *Barāʾa* (Chapter 9). Its name *Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad* likewise points to its purpose, when one reflects upon the whole chapter and what it calls for of the many subtle and abundant meanings of absolution.

**[p. 345]** This chapter is the greatest source of monotheism in the Qur'an. Al-Rāzī said: "Monotheism is a station that the scope of speech cannot contain, for when you report about the Truth there is a reporter, a thing reported about, and the report itself; together these make three. Thus the intellect recognises it, but speech cannot reach it." Al-Junayd was asked about monotheism and said: "It is a state in which traces vanish, sciences become confused, and Allah is as He has always been." Al-Junayd also said: "The noblest utterance on monotheism is that of al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him): 'Glory be to Him who has not given His creation any path to knowing Him except through incapacity to know Him.'"

*"In the name of Allah"*, who possesses all perfection through majesty and beauty. *"Al-Raḥmān"*, who from His bounty pours out the universal gifts upon all existents. *"Al-Raḥīm"*, who singles out the people of His love with the light of favour, in completion and perfection.

When *al-Kawthar* was the reason for forbidding what the denial (of the Prophet) contained of evil deeds, and it was known from it that he (ﷺ) is specially favoured with good, which implies that his hater is the one cut off (*al-abtar*), the question arose as to what he should do with those who hate him, whether to fight them or to leave them. So *al-Kāfirūn* came for the matter of leaving them, because the people of the religion were few at that time. This is an indication that this world is founded upon causes. From *al-Kāfirūn* it was known that the hater is not to be regarded; so the soul was moved to ask about the time of readiness for fighting after this leaving, and about what follows from fighting in terms of actually subduing the hater. Thus *Sūrat al-Naṣr* came for that, indicating that this is not to be asked about, as to when it will occur, so as to fit the good manner of submission. Rather one should ask only about what he should do at its coming, in worship and good conduct. It expresses this with the particle of certainty, informing that it is surely coming, so asking about its time is not the habit of the travellers.

When the treasures of these hoards became manifest through the subtleties of those symbols, together with the apparent indications joined to them, the condition of Abū Lahab was called to mind, for in him, despite his close kinship, there was extreme hostility and great striving against everything opposed to the noblest of servants. The longing grew intense to know whether his condition would change at that time, through repentance, which the *Naṣr* chapter ended with, or whether he would be abandoned and turned over to the greatest loss and sin. So his chapter came clearly for that, because wretchedness had overcome him, and he descended to its depths, barred from ascending the lofty steps of elevation. When Allah, glory be to Him, made clear by that the destruction of His enemy (ﷺ), and concluded with the foremost of his enemies, He judged his destruction and that of his wife, a destruction without remedy, in a manifest way, showing that he was in the lowest degrees of baseness and the greatest kind of loss. The intellect danced with delight at these matters, and the mind became intoxicated by the wonders of what is decreed. **[p. 347]** The listener was stirred to the utmost stirring by describing the Doer of this, which is beyond human capacity and breaks customary norms: the manifesting of one single person over all people, despite their intense enmity towards him. *Al-Ikhlāṣ* came revealing the greatness that was established for the friend of the Prophet (ﷺ), glory be to Him and exalted, who commanded him with this religion and performed for him these great matters, which should be a reason for whoever has a heart or gives ear while being present, so that He would not be thought of as finding anything of that, or anything else, difficult. The representation of everything that commands His Lord, whatever has been and will be, in whatever manner, is conformity to His command and obedience to Him, and is an informing of the true belief which necessitated this victory, bearing upon all the sects of error. This – in the connection of the latter to the former with respect to the chapters – is among the greatest correspondences in this regard, considering the verses: that He, glory be to Him, explained with *al-Fīl* and what follows it of chapters the verses of *al-Fātiḥa* entire, [then] from the beginning of *al-Baqara* to the verse of monotheism. Thus with *al-Fīl* He indicated that He combines the attributes of perfection, that to Him belongs praise for guarding His House from kings and protecting it from the plots of tyrants, and for nurturing Quraysh in the best way, those who are the noblest of the worlds; with their righteousness the righteousness of their land, *Umm al-Qurā*, is established, and with its righteousness the righteousness of its inhabitants. This shows that He judges **[p. 348]** the servants on the Day of Summoning. For this reason He gave the leader of the guided the religion which singled out worship and seeking help for Him, and gave him *al-Kawthar*, guided him to the straight path, and protected him from the path of the stubborn disbelievers and the astray. At the beginning of *al-Baqara* He indicated that the God-fearing – for whom the Book is guidance – enter the religion in multitudes. The richest and most obstinate of the disbelievers, for whom warning and its absence are equal in that they will not believe, is Abū Lahab, and whoever travels his path, whether openly or secretly; loss encompasses them and destruction and ruin overtake them, by the judgment of the One, the Subduer, who is to be worshipped and made One in the all-encompassing verse of the calls to monotheism: *"O people, worship your Lord"* (2:21), who is characterised by what is in *Sūrat al-Ṣamad*, the like of which has not been sent down describing Him. Thus the religion was completed at that point, through what belongs to Him, glory be to Him, of perfect attributes and majestic descriptions, with might and gentleness. Nothing remained but seeking refuge for the people of the religion from any flaw entering upon them, or from any uprooting or slipping. So He concluded with the two *Muʿawwidhatayn* for that purpose. And Allah is the one asked, in bestowing the granting of the sought-after to every seeker.

* *

Since the purpose of the Qur'an is to call the servants to the One worshipped, and the one called to something most needs to know it, and since definition is sometimes of the Essence, sometimes of the attributes, and sometimes of the acts, and since this *ummah* was **[p. 349]** the noblest of nations, because its Prophet is the highest of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, and it is the seal, the Qur'an expounded at length its definition of Him, glory be to Him, and carried the explanation of that to a point beyond which there is no increase, and no earlier scripture came near it in this. However, since the great, when its greatness is absolute, its essence is hard to know, and since Allah, exalted be He, is the Greatest absolutely, and since knowledge of His Essence – as al-Ghazālī indicated in *al-Jawāhir*, and al-Fakhr al-Rāzī in his books – is the narrowest in scope, the most difficult in speech, the most disobedient to thought in attainment, and the furthest from accepting remembrance in free flow, the Qur'an contains of that only hints and allusions, most of which return to mentioning absolute transcendence, as in His saying, exalted be He, *"There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing"* (42:11), and to absolute exaltation, as in His saying, *"Glory be to Him, exalted above what they describe"* (6:100). The analogy would have been to limit itself to that, together with definition by attributes and acts. But since this *ummah* stood at the peak of goodness of understanding, in addition to the nobility it had attained, Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, bestowed upon it *Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ* complete, with an exposition such that human intellects cannot bear any addition to it. That is by explaining that He is established with an establishment unlike any other establishment, in a way that belongs to no other at all; and that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is far removed from likeness, equal, counterpart, and peer; He has no spouse and no child, and He has no need of anyone in any way **[p. 350]**; rather to Him belong creation and command, so He destroys whom He wills and makes happy whom He wishes. He said, commanding His Prophet (ﷺ), so that it would be the first word in which His message is indicated, as a reply to whoever denied him personally, and to the Brahmins who say that reason is sufficient without the messengers, and so that the explanation would be carried upon his tongue (ﷺ), so that the understanding of creation of those lofty attributes would be closer to them, due to the affinity they have with it: *"Say"* – that is, O most noble of creation, and none understands fully from its Sender other than you. The command is given without restriction to a particular hearer, to indicate the generality of the message, and that the intended meaning is everyone to whom it can be said, whether he is actually asking about that or only potentially, as an urging to call to mind what belongs to the Lord of this religion – which He has so surrounded and so nurtured – of greatness and majesty, grandeur and perfection. In the absolute address, which points to generality, there is a refutation of whoever acknowledges his sending (ﷺ) only to the Arabs, and it shows that the one to whom the saying is addressed is not harmed by it, for its outward meanings are understood by everyone and there is no temptation in them in any way. Temptation comes only **[p. 351]** when the misguided one delves into what his intellect cannot bear.

Since the most important of the aims is the refutation of the *muʿaṭṭila* (deniers of divine attributes), who are a kind of those who say: *"We die and live, and nothing destroys us but time"* (45:24), He established His existence in the most complete, highest, fullest and clearest way, with a meaning that amounts to this: that His reality is established with an establishment toward which no doubt can be directed in any way. So He said, unveiling secrets – for it is impossible for Him to be absent from them at all – and for the bewildered: *"He"*. He began with this noble name, which is the most inward of names, indicating that He has concealed the hidden with respect to His Essence, like the *alif*, and that He is necessarily existent in Himself, and that His identity is not derived from anything other than Himself nor dependent upon anything other than Himself. For whatever has its identity derived from another or dependent upon it, when that other is not taken into account, it is not itself; but whatever has its identity from its own essence, it is itself, whether another is taken into account or not. Therefore no one deserves this name but Him, absolutely. Moreover, the letter *hā'* alone, by being one of the innermost letters of the throat, indicates that He is the First and the Hidden, who originated what is other than Himself; and the *wāw*, by being one of the more outward letters of the lips, indicates that He is the Last and the Manifest, and that the end is to Him, and there is no goal beyond Him, and that He is the Originator and the Restorer. This is indicated by the repetition of the *wāw* in its name, and by His encompassing everything, by reason of the encompassing that is in it **[p. 352]**.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 112, verse 1 (part 2 of 5):

Since His existence, glory be to Him, is through His own essence and is not derived from anything else, whatever has its existence derived from something else is contingent (*mumkin*). The reality of His name, which is His very identity (*huwa huwa*), cannot be explained. No name for the reality of anything else can be formed from a genus (*jins*), a species (*naw'*), or a differentia (*fasl*), because He has no genus, no species, and no cause (*sabab*) by which He is known. What has no cause cannot be known except through its necessary attributes (*lawazim*). These attributes are of two kinds: negative (*salbiyya*) and relational (*idafiyya*). Some are near and some are distant. Defining Him through the relational and the near attributes is more complete than defining Him through the negative and the distant ones. The distant attribute is like laughter, which is the attribute that follows the one who marvels, in relation to humanity. It is not the effect of a thing but the effect of its effect. Combining the negative and the relational is more complete than relying on only one of them. For this reason a name was chosen that comprises both kinds, so that the definition would be more complete. That name is the fact that this identity is God (*ilah*). So a name denoting it was chosen, and it is specific and not shared. It is the first of the manifestations of the pronoun, just as the hamza is the first of the manifestations of the alif. For this reason some have said: "The Greatest Name is the last of the outward names." For this reason all the names are attributes of Him, and He is the first of the inward realities. So He said, unveiling Himself to spirits and to those who affirm His oneness (*muwahhidun*): ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the Existent, besides whom there is truly no existent. He is the one named by this name. This name was chosen for reporting about Him because it denotes all the attributes of perfection: majesty (*jalal*) and beauty (*jamal*). It is also because it is a name that comprises all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names. It is the nearest of the necessary attributes to the identity, because it has no necessary attribute nearer to it than necessary existence (*wujub al-wujud*), which is required by the essence together with the attributes it has, without any intermediary. Through the necessity of His existence He bestows existence by His choice upon everything He wills. The totality of necessity, which is purely negative, is by itself the bestowal of existence, which is a choice of generosity (*jud*) combined with existence and the attribution of divinity (*uluhiyya*), which majesty (*jalala*) encompasses. This is the nearest of the necessary attributes to the Most Holy Essence. The expression of it indicates that there is nothing constituting the identity, neither a genus nor anything else, nor a cause. Otherwise, turning from it to defining Him through a necessary attribute would be deficient. It also indicates that His divinity extends absolutely to all existents. So describing that identity through the necessary attribute is the most eloquent eloquence and the most precise wisdom, because it, together with being the Truth, points to the subtleties that were mentioned.

When the essence was mentioned, which has no cause and no constituent, neither genus, species, nor anything else at all, but is pure unity and transcendence above composition, having no plurality and no duality in any respect, and when He defined it by the name that comprises the kinds of negations and relations that are necessary to it, which is the nearest of the necessary attributes to it, its specific existence was made clear as it is. So that was a complete definition, because defining what has no composition through its near necessary attributes in perfection is like defining composite things through their constituents. The complete definition is that a form corresponding to the intelligible reality comes to be in the soul. Adding explanation was desirable because it is more perfect, especially in hidden and inward matters. He followed that with a negative name as a sign that in this world our gaze toward the side of majesty should be greater, and that name's nearness to majesty is like its nearness to the identity. It denotes complete and pure unity, and it is the descent of majesty just as majesty is the descent of the identity. Just as majesty has no sharing in it at all, it resembles it in that there is no sharing in it for anyone else, may He be exalted, when it is used alone in its true meaning. In the negation there is an indication that everything other than Him, glory be to Him, is nonexistence. So He said, unveiling Himself to hearts and to the knowers of God (*'arifun*), refuting the Christians who speak of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the Jews who say He is a body, the Magians who say He is two, a light that creates good and a darkness that creates evil, the Sabians who worship the stars, and the polytheists who believe in the divinity of idols, reporting a further report, or as a substitute for majesty, or as the predicate of an omitted subject: ﴿One﴾. Because it is specific in affirmation when He is alone, the knowledge of "one" (*ahad*) is a definite noun that does not need the article "al-". It is more ancient in indicating the attributes of majesty, just as the name Allah is more ancient in indicating the attributes of perfection. The true One is the one whose essence is transcendent above all modes of composition and plurality, and above anything that entails either of them, such as corporeality, spatiality, or sharing in a reality and its properties, such as necessary existence, complete power, and perfect wisdom, which require divinity, without entailing circularity or infinite regress from the side of composition or anything else. It was read with the omission of "say" (*qul*) here and in the two protective surahs (al-Mu'awwidhatayn), while there is agreement on its affirmation in al-Kafirun and its negation in Tabbat. The likely wisdom is that al-Kafirun is addressed to the disbelievers with what lies between hostility and disengagement, so it suited the situation for it to be from him ﷺ. Tabbat is a rebuke and a reproach to the Messenger's ﷺ uncle, so it is not fitting for that to come from the Prophet ﷺ. The enduring good deeds (*al-baqiyat*) are what lie between monotheism and seeking refuge, so it was fitting that he be commanded to convey it and to call upon God with it. He placed oneness (*ahadiyya*) after divinity (*uluhiyya*) and not the reverse, because divinity is an expression of His independence from all and the need of all for Him. Whatever is like this is absolutely one, otherwise it would need its parts. So divinity by its nature requires unity, but unity does not require divinity. He expressed it this way and not as "one" (*wahid*) because the purpose is to attribute unity to a degree beyond which nothing can be more. Ibn Sina said that "one" is predicated of what falls under it by gradation (*tashkik*). What is not divisible in any respect at all is more fitting for oneness than what is divisible in some respects, and what is divisible intellectually is more fitting than what is divisible by the senses, and what is divisible by the senses potentially is more fitting than what is divisible by the senses actually. Since it is established that unity is capable of being more or less intense...

[p. 357] And the one (al-wahid) is predicated of what falls under it by gradation (tashkik, predication admitting degrees of more and less). The most perfect in unity is that which no other thing can exceed in it. Otherwise it would not reach the ultimate aim. The word ahad (One) comprises all of this and indicates unity in every respect, and that there is no multiplicity whatsoever there: neither a conceptual multiplicity of constituents, such as genera and differentiae, nor intellectual parts, such as matter and form, nor a sensory multiplicity in potency or act, as in bodies. This is because He, glorified be He, is exalted above genus, differentia, matter, form, accidents, portions, limbs, shapes, colours, and all the other aspects of plurality that would mar the complete and true unity, which is befitting to the nobility of His Face and the might of His majesty. Nothing may resemble Him or be equal to Him, because whatever's identity is achieved through the aggregation of parts has its identity dependent upon the existence of those parts. Thus it is not essentially itself but through another. Therefore He is exalted above multiplicity in every respect and characterised by unity in every aspect. This arrangement (nazm) has thus reached the greatest magnitude in eloquent expression. Glorified is He who sent down this speech: how great is its station, and how overpowering is its authority! He is the ultimate of needs, and from Him is the attainment of requests. The highest descriptions of those who describe Him, and the greatest attributes of those who ascribe attributes to Him, do not reach the least of what He has singled out of majesty, greatness and splendour. Rather, the possible measure of it, which is impossible to exceed, is what He mentioned in His Mighty Book and deposited in His holy and wise revelation. Through discussing its meaning and the meaning of "One" (wahid), what preceded is established. The Imam Abu al-'Abbas al-Iqlishi said in his commentary on the Names: Among the people of the language, some equated the two and made them synonyms. Some of them said: the root of ahad is wahid, from which the alif was dropped, and then the hamza replaced the open waw. [Some of them said: its root is not wahid, although both have one meaning; rather its root is waḥida (from unity, wahda), yaḥidu, so he is waḥd,] like ḥasan, yuḥsinu, fa-huwa ḥasan (from ḥusn), the waw being replaced by a hamza. As for those who distinguished between them, some said: aḥad is a name in its own right, with no substitution or alteration in it. Others said: its root is waḥada, and the waw was replaced by a hamza. End of quotation. I have extracted the discussion of the two noble names from several commentaries on the Beautiful Names and others, including the commentary of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, Fakhr al-Din al-Harrali, and others. They said: the One in which there is no multiplicity in any way, neither by division nor otherwise, together with the attribute of greatness, so as to exclude the indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard, the partless particle in kalam theology). [It too] is that which cannot be doubled (la yatathanna), that is, it has no opposite and no like. Thus He, glorified be He, is One in both senses absolutely, not relatively, in any condition or thing. The Imam Abu al-'Abbas al-Iqlishi said in his commentary on the Names: This is the reality of unity according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun). Thus nothing composite may be described by it except metaphorically, as when you say: "a single man" (rajul wahid) or "a single dirham" (dirham wahid). It is only truly predicated of what has no part, such as the indivisible atom according to the Ash'aris. However, when you consider and find that its existence is from another, you know that its deserving of this attribute is not like the deserving of its originator for it. It too is described by it only because of its insignificance, whereas its Originator, glorified be He, is described by it together with the attribute of greatness. So His being described with unity absolutely, and the atom's being described with unity by considering the absence of composition from body, is different, since the validity of its being described as a part removes from it the reality of that. Unity, also, considered in the second sense, which is that which has no equal, is truly valid only for Him, glorified be He. Everything whose species is identical with its individual, such as the Throne, the Chair, the sun and the moon, can have equals assumed for it. It has a third meaning, which is singularity in act and origination, so that He does whatever He wills without depending on anything. The difference between this aspect and the one before it is that the first looks to the negation of a second god, while this one denies a specific helper and minister. Both are essential negative attributes. The upshot is that [p. 359] sound reasoning shows that for us there is one originator, in the sense that no deficiency of division can befall Him in any respect, and in the sense that He has no equal in any consideration, and in the sense that He is sole in act, independent in origination, singular in disposal, and single in direction. The witness of the reason protected from the darkness of desire and the density of nature has decided this, and the decisive transmitted texts and the explicit hearing have related it. For this reason the most important truth is His call to all creation, and the call of His Seal Messenger (ﷺ) was to all creatures. The Proof of Islam, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, said at the end of his commentary on the Names, in explaining the reduction of the many names to one essence and seven attributes: The Ahad is that from which an equal is negated. He also said in the aforementioned commentary: The One is that which is not divisible and not doubled. As for what is not divisible, it is like the single substance that is not divided. He said: it is One in the sense that it has no part, and for this reason the point has no part. And God the Exalted is One in the sense that it is impossible to assume division in His essence. As for what is not doubled, it is that which has no equal, such as the sun for instance, for although it is capable of division in imagination and is located in its own essence, because it belongs to the category of bodies, it has no equal, though it is possible that it could have one. There is no existent in existence which is singular in the specificity of its existence with a singularity that cannot be conceived of as being shared by anything else at all, except the One who is absolute, from eternity to eternity. A servant is one only when he has no equal among the members of his kind in any quality of goodness. This is relative to the members of his kind, and relative to time, since it is possible that there could be another like him at another time, and relative to some qualities but not all. So there is no unity absolutely except for God the Exalted. [p. 360] The Imam Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Shahrastani said in the introduction to his book al-Milal wa al-Nihal: They differed concerning the One: is it part of the number, or is it the principle of number and not included within number? This disagreement arises from the homonymy of the word "one." The one is used to mean that from which number is composed, for two has no meaning except one repeated at the first repetition, and likewise three and four. It is also used to mean that from which number arises, that is, it is its cause, and it is not included in counting, that is, number is not composed of it. The oneness (wahidiyya) is accompanied by all numbers, not in that number is composed of them, but also every existent is its genus, species or individual, and is one: one says "one human" and "one person." And within number too, since three is in that it is three, one. So the one in the first sense is included in number, in the second sense is the cause of number, and in the third sense is accompanying number. There is no category among the three that is applied to the Creator, may He be exalted, the meaning of which is: He is one, not like the units (ahad), by which is meant these units and multiplicity originated from Him, and division in any of its aspects is impossible for Him. End of quotation. He is also one in Himself, not relative to a second in any respect. [p. 361] Some of them said: the one indicates eternity and primacy, for the one among numbers is their pillar and the manifestation of their beginning. The ahad indicates His distinction from His creation in all His attributes, and the negation of the modes of association from Him. So ahad is formed to negate what is mentioned with it of number, while wahid is a name for the beginning of number. The Imam Abu Hatim Muhammad ibn Mahran al-Razi said in his book al-Zina: Some of the wise said: He, may He be exalted, is called "One" only because He, mighty and majestic, has not ceased before creation, singular in eternity, with no second with Him and no creation. Then He originated creation, and all of creation, despite its need for Him, glorified be He, came to be in need of one another, holding each other, mutually hostile, opposed, similar, paired, connected and separated. He, mighty and majestic, is independent of creatures and does not need anything, so that such a thing would be associated with Him by His need of it, nor does anything oppose Him so that such a thing would be an opponent of His by its contesting with Him, thereby making that opponent and companion a second. Rather, He is singular in His independence from all His creation, for He was before everything. Primacy indicates unity. So "One" is a name indicating one order, known by its name to be one, with nothing before it: "And in everything there is for Him a sign / that indicates that He is One." [p. 362] The one among numbers in calculation has nothing before it; rather it is before every number and is outside number. The one, however you turn it, nothing is added to it and nothing subtracted from it. You say: one times one by one, and nothing is added to the one. This shows that nothing is before it. And when it shows that nothing is before it, it shows that it is the originator of things. When it shows that it is the originator of things, it shows that it is the one who makes things independent. When it is the one who makes things independent, it shows that nothing is after it. When there is nothing before it nor after it, it is the singular in eternity, meaning the One who has no equal. So it is the Ahad. He said: For this reason it is said: He is One and Ahad. We have said that ahad is a name more complete, that is more general, than wahid. Do you not see that when you say: "So-and-so is not withstood by one (wahid)," it may mean that two or three or more can withstand him? But when you say: "So-and-so is not withstood by anyone (ahad)," you have affirmed definitively that neither one nor two nor more can withstand him. Thus ahad is more complete than wahid. In ahad there is a particularity that is not in wahid. You say: "There is not one (wahid) in the house," which may mean one of the animals, birds, beasts, or humans, so wahid encompasses people and non-people. But when you say: "There is not anyone (ahad) in the house," it is specific to human beings and not others. Ahad is excluded from entering into multiplication, into number, into division, [p. 363] and into anything of calculation, and it is singular in the quality of ahadiyya. Wahid, however, submits to number and division, and other things fall within calculation. You say: one, two, three. This, although it is not of the number, is the cause of number and is included in number, because when you multiply one by one it does not increase, and two is the root of calculation. You say, regarding division: one between two or three, so that each of the two has a half, and each of the three a third. This is division. Ahad is excluded from this. One does not say "ahad and two," nor "ahad times ahad," nor "ahad in one," nor "ahad in two or three." The wahid, though it is not divisible into one, is divisible into two, three and what exceeds them. You say: "one part of two parts or three or more." It is not permissible to say: "a part of ahad out of two parts or more." God has named Himself Wahid and Ahad, and described Himself with oneness (wahdaniyya) and singularity (ahadiyya). So wahid is a description that necessarily belongs to Him in reality, because He was before, and there was no second with Him. Two is the consequence of one. Thus He is wahid because He is united in eternity, and creation is two because it is joined with origination, for origination is second to eternity, and by it duality appeared. So the one is ahad in His essence: there is nothing before Him, nor from anything, nor in anything, nor upon anything, nor for anything, nor with anything, so that that thing would be a second with Him. Rather He is the one who brings into being, and all things belong to Him, [p. 364] and He is the one united in His essence, impossible to have anything second to Him in any respect, and all creation belongs to Him. Even if He is called by the name "one," or even if this attribute has necessarily belonged to all things in one respect, it is removed from them in another respect.

As it is said: "one man," "one horse," and "one camel." The same is said of all other things. This is a quality that attaches to the word, and the thing named cannot be free of many meanings gathered together in it, such as body and accident. It is a unity composed of scattered things, and every thing is not free of pairing, opposition, similarity, and limit or number. All these attributes negate from Him the meaning of uniqueness and oneness. The Arabs have many dialects for "one." It is said: wahid, ahad, wahd, wahid, hadd, uhad, muwahhad, and awhad. All of these return to the meaning of "one," though there are subtle meanings within them. Nothing is used to describe Allah, Mighty and Majestic, except al-Wahid and al-Ahad. I say: al-Wahid, according to some i'rab (grammatical readings), occurs in Surat al-Muddaththir. He said: All of them are derived from al-Wahid. It seems that this is derived from hadd (limit). As if all things end at Him, and all of them are limited, other than Him, Mighty and Majestic, while He is not limited. Rather, He is the ultimate end of all those who are limited, and the end of all ends, with no end for Him. Al-Ahad in speech comes with the meaning of "first" and with the meaning of "one." When it comes with the meaning of "first" and with the meaning of "one," it is permissible to use it in affirmative statements, as in your saying: "This is one, unique." The Arabs used to call Sunday in the Jahiliyyah "first" (yawm al-ahad). Your saying "yawm al-ahad" is evidence that it is the first day of the week, and "al-ithnayn" (Monday) is evidence that it is the second day. In the Torah, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, first created "the day of al-Ahad" among the days. I say: It is possible that the meaning of "yawm al-ahad" is "the day of Allah," which was attributed to Him because it was the first of His created days. When He brought the second into existence, it was called "the day of al-ithnayn," because it was the second day after the day of al-Ahad. He said: The opposite of wahid is ithnan (two), and the opposite of ahad is "the other" (al-akhar). Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿One of them said, "Indeed, I see myself pressing wine."﴾ [Yusuf: 36], then He said of its opposite: "and the other said." This is evidence that the meaning of their saying "yawm al-ahad" is the first day, for they said for what follows it "two," and did not say "the other." For when ahad does not mean "first," its opposite is "the other." When ahad means "first," it is permissible in affirmation and in negation. When it does not mean "first" but means "one," it is permissible in affirmation and permissible in negation. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿So send one of you with this silver of yours﴾ [al-Kahf: 19]. This is from affirmation. When ahad means neither "first" nor "one," it is not permissible to use it except in negation. You say: "No one came to me" (ma ja'anī ahad), and it is not permissible to say: "Someone came to me" (ja'anī ahad) or "Someone spoke to me" (kallamanī ahad). Allah, Exalted, said in the sense of negation: ﴿Does he think that no one will have power over him?﴾ [al-Balad: 5]. Ahad is used for both masculine and feminine. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any of the women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32].

As for wahid, it does not apply equally to masculine and feminine until the ta' marbuta (ha') is added, so it is said "wahidah." It is not permissible to say "like one of the women" (ka-wahid min al-nisa'). Ahad may also mean plural. The Arabs say: "One of us may go days without eating," meaning "all of us do not eat." Thus it carries the meaning of both the singular and the group. End of quotation. Therefore, wahid is among the relational affirmative names. In the basic usage of the language, relative to a second, it is half of it, and relative to a third, it is a third of it. Likewise, it is an attribute of Allah, Exalted, meaning the one who is singular in being characterized by divinity, such that nothing else can share it in any way. Thus He has no partner. Ahad is among the negative attributes, indeed it is the collection of them. He is ahad in Himself; He does not accept number or composition in any way, neither by division nor otherwise, whether He is considered in relation to others or not. Thus it is purely negation. It is an attribute returning to the very essence, in the sense that He is perfect in His essence, and considering anything does not affect its concept at all. Fard (singular) looks to the negation of number. Thus the three attributes differ, even though they are close in meaning.

Imam Abu al-Khayr al-Qazwini al-Shafi'i said in his book "al-'Urwa al-Wuthqa fi Usul al-Din," quoting some who distinguished it from wahid: "Ahad is a name for negating what is mentioned with it." Some of them said that it is the One for whom partition is not permissible, neither in act nor in imagination. He is ahad in His essence and ahad in His attributes. Allah's declaring Himself one is His knowledge that He is one, and His informing about that. The servant's affirming the oneness of Allah is his knowledge of that along with his acknowledgment of it.

Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi said in "Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna" (Explanation of the Beautiful Names): Allah, glorified and exalted, is ahad in His essence, ahad in His attributes, ahad in His acts, ahad not from anything, not divisible nor partible, ahad not composed nor compound, ahad whom nothing resembles and who resembles nothing, ahad who is independent of every one. End of quotation.

This is the meaning of what the grammarians transmitted from Tha'lab, that he distinguished between them: wahid admits number, while ahad does not admit it. It is said: "Allah is ahad," and it is not said: "Zayd is ahad," because ahad is a specificity of Allah, Exalted. Zayd can have states. He objected to this with a counted number that is conjoined: it is said "ahad wa-'ishrun" and "ithnan wa-'ishrun." He answered that ahad here has the meaning of wahid.

Fakhr al-Din said in "Sharh al-Asma'": It is specific to the Creator, glorified, while wahid allows sharing. For this reason it is stripped of the definite article (al-), because it became an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, specifically, so it became definite.

Al-Azhari said: Ahmad ibn Yahya was asked about al-ahad (the plural form "al-uhad"), whether it is the plural of ahad. He said: "Far be it from God. Ahad has no plural." It is not far-fetched to say that it is the plural of wahid, like "al-ashhad," the plural of shahid. End of quotation.

Al-Iqlishi said in "Sharh al-Asma'": Al-Ahad is the one who is neither divided nor partible. Thus it is, according to this, a name for the very essence, in which the plurality is negated from His essence. He is thereby sanctified by this attribute from the attributes of bodies, which are susceptible to division and partition, and from the point and the indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard), according to those who affirm them among the theologians (mutakallimun). The simple substance (al-jawhar al-basit) is according to those who claim it among the philosophers. Although these are not divisible and are not partible, they contradict the Creator in His oneness (uhudiyyah). As for the point, some hold it to be an accident, since it is the extremity of a line, and if the line is an accident, the point is more deserving of accidentality. As for the indivisible atom, although it is not divisible, it is measured by a part, and whatever is measured by a part does not escape the states of existence; it is, however it is, according to the view of those who affirm it among the theologians, although they dispute its attributes, and it does not escape accidents. As for the simple substance according to those who affirm it, its existence for them is not its essence, if we make it two, and what it is in this description according to them has duality. Thus the Creator, glorified and exalted, is distinguished by His oneness from these existents, just as He is distinguished in His essence from bodies. His existence is from His essence, and His attributes are not other than His essence. As for wahid, it is an attribute of His essence, in which the negation of a partner and an equal from Him is included. They differ, meaning that ahad looks to the essence itself, while wahid looks to a matter outside of it.

Al-Bayhaqi said in "Kitab al-Asma' wa-l-Sifat": Ahad, in what the polytheists call a god besides Him, is not permissible to be a god, since the signs of createdness, such as divisibility and finitude, are present in it and necessary for it, while the Creator, glorified and exalted, is not divisible and not finite. It has passed that ahad is specific to Allah, glorified and exalted. There is no difference in applying it to Him, glorified and exalted, between its being definite and indefinite, because it is definite in itself. Thus the objection of some heretics (mulhidun) is void: "The name Allah is definite, while ahad is indefinite and cannot be used as an attribute."

Even if we concede this, it is permissible to make it a substitute (badal), as has been mentioned before, and there is no obstacle to substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one, like ﴿We will surely seize him by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 15–16]. The author of "Kitab al-Zina" said: Upon this reading, that is, the reading with tanwin (indefiniteness), the community agreed. A group narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq that he recited: "Say: He is Allah, the One (al-Wahid), the Ahad, al-Samad."

Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said in "Sharh al-Asma' al-Husna": Ahad is a name which Allah made the intellects unable to grasp in terms of its sign in creation affirmatively. The Arabs never used it alone, meaning in its true sense, not with the meaning of "one" or "first," for example, except in negation, because they knew that it expresses an all-encompassing comprehensiveness from which nothing escapes. That is among what intellects and senses perceive in negation but do not perceive in affirmation. So they say: "There is no one (ahad) in the house," as a negation of all. It is not admissible in their minds to say: "There is someone (ahad) in the house or in existence," since in their understanding there is no human being who comprises every human. When His name appeared in the Qur'an from Allah, the believers received it with faith, and their hearts loved the surah that mentions Him, for it gathers the countless praises of the Most Merciful. It is one of the three lights in the Qur'an, [the Qur'an is] a light.

And the light of His light [sūrah]: He mentioned *al-Aḥad* (the One) at its end, and *Āyat al-Kursī* (the Throne Verse) at its beginning, and Sūrat Yā-Sīn, which comes before it, in its place relative to it. [The verse] "One" is an explicit indication of the Name of God, who encompasses everything, and no association (*shirk*) reaches Him, whether true or false. And "One" is an explicit indication of the Name of the Deity (*al-Ilāh*), to which association cannot truly apply, though it may apply falsely: "and they have taken gods besides God" (Qur'an 21:24, paraphrased in the source). This is because "one" implies a "second," whereas *Aḥad* is all-inclusive and encompassing, leaving nothing outside of it that could be paired with it. That is, its meaning looks to His being, glorified and exalted, now as He was in pre-eternity, alone. Creation is perishing, so in reality it is non-existent, as if it had never been, because it is encompassed by Him, is in His grip, and is subject to His will. There is therefore no "outside" that could be a counterpart to Him, since nothing is paired with something except a rival in equality, or a contender in opposition, or otherwise. Everything, in relation to Him, is non-existent: "Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die" (Qur'an 39:30); "Everything upon it perishes" (Qur'an 55:26); "Everything is perishing except His Face" (Qur'an 28:88). [This is His intent,] as evidenced by what precedes and follows it, so there is no ambiguity in it for the people of unity (*ahl al-waḥda*), upon whom be disgrace and curse.

He said: Unity (*waḥda*), derived from "one," is the [ultimate] limit, the end beyond which there is nothing further. Whatever falls short of the unity that is the end is secondary, and below it. The totality of all these encompassings, high and low, is *al-Uḥdiyya* (absolute oneness), from which no deviant strays and out of which no one departs. Among the Names are those known to some of His creatures according to what has been given to them of Him, such as *al-Raḥīm* (the Merciful) and *al-ʿAlīm* (the All-Knowing). Among them are those that their vicegerency cannot attain, such as the Names mentioned earlier from His Name *al-Muḥṣī* (the Counter), though they attain a likeness of them in their own words. And among them are those that knowledge has not reached and minds have not grasped the like of, and that is His Name *al-Aḥad*. So God is the One (*al-Aḥad*) besides whom there is no one (*aḥad*), and that concludes the passage.

Abū al-Ḥakam ibn Burjān said in his commentary on the Beautiful Names: "It [*al-Aḥad*], that is, is the root of the chapter of unity (*al-waḥda*), and indicates pure unity. Do you not see that it is a negation, which comes with it? When you say, 'No one (*aḥad*) came to me,' both two are negated. But you do not say, 'One (*aḥad*) came to me' as you say, 'A single one (*wāḥid*) came to me,' because a single one loses its singularity when a second is added to it. By contrast, *al-Uḥdiyya* (absolute oneness) is an inseparable property of the One; its rule does not leave it even after a second is added. Rather, it has a protected aspect, which becomes evident through even and odd numbers. For you say: 'No one (*aḥad*) came to me,' and so both even and odd are negated. This is evidence of its increased nobility, for whenever a Name's indication becomes obscure, its knowledge becomes difficult to attain, and its knowledge escapes the minds, that is evidence of its nearness to the Greatest Name (*al-Ism al-Aʿẓam*)." 

Some of the knowers (*al-ʿārifīn*) said, in disclosing the meaning of *al-Aḥad* and its rank: the Greatest Essence is pure hiddenness, and *al-Aḥad* is the first of its determinations (*taʿayyunāt*). For this reason it begins with the *hamza*, which is the first determination of the *alif*, the *alif* being pure blaze. That is the secret of its difference from the letters, in that every letter indicates its named thing, but the first letter of its name is [of the *alif*]... except the *alif*, because it is hidden. So the first letter of its name is the *hamza*, which is the first of its determinations, and the *hamza*, being elevated toward the hiddenness of the *alif*, was the first of its name too, not indicating its named thing.

Then, after determination by the all-encompassing, all-pervading oneness (*al-Uḥdiyya*), it descends to the divinity (*al-Ilāhiyya*), and from it to singularity (*al-Wāḥidiyya*). For this reason *al-Wāḥid* begins with the *wāw*, which is a link to what is in it of the *alif* that is hidden. For the single one is elevated to understanding the Deity (*al-Ilāh*), the Deity is elevated to apprehending *al-Aḥad*, and *al-Aḥad* is elevated to the worship of the Most Holy, Most Transcendent Essence. Whoever believes in His oneness, glorified and exalted, will have produced from that love and magnification of Him, and that is the affirmation of divinity (*tawḥīd al-Ulūhiyya*), since singling Him out in this respect requires perfection and beauty. And God is the Granter of success.

Imām Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr said: When the purpose of the Mighty Book was concluded in its entirety, the matter returned to what it was, and informed the scholar of their condition, of their oscillation between two non-existences: "Then God brings forth the final creation" (Qur'an 29:20). Their existence is from Him, glorified and exalted, their continuance is by Him, and they, and everything that issues from them of their words and deeds, all of that is His creation and invention. He, glorified and exalted, was, and there was no world, no time, and no place; and He is now as He was. He has no need of anyone and requires no specific [place], He is not bound by time, and He is not confined by place. So praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, the Possessor of praise and deserving of it absolutely; to Him belongs praise in this world and the next, to Him belongs the judgment, and to Him is the return: "Say: He is God, One" (Qur'an 112:1); "God, the Eternal Refuge" (Qur'an 112:2); "He begets not, nor is He begotten" (Qur'an 112:3); "And there is none comparable to Him" (Qur'an 112:4). He is the true Existent, and His speech is truth. "And the life of this world is but play and amusement; and the Abode of the Hereafter is better for those who fear God" (Qur'an 6:32). Blessed is the one who sought clarity from the Book of God, approached the matter from its proper gate, knew himself and his worldly life, answered the caller of God, and saw no true agent in existence except Him, glorified and exalted. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

When the purpose of the Book was complete, and the magnitude of God's mercy toward whoever reflects, takes heed, and turns in repentance became clear, it was the place to seek refuge and protection from the evil of the envious and the plots of enemies. So it concluded with the two protectors (*al-Muʿawwidhatayn*), [seeking refuge] from the evil of what He created and produced, and the evil of the two worlds (humans and jinn). That concludes the passage.

(p-374) When the explanation of His essence, glory be to Him and exalted, was complete in this manner, which He indicated through oneness (*ahadiyya*, the state of being absolutely one), marked by transcendence above division and likeness, and since the explanation of the Qur'an reached the utmost limits of explanation, and since *al-Ahad* is among the descriptions that go deepest into negation, and since association can occur in its use in negation in its true meaning, and association can occur in its use in affirmation and negation alike, or its indication of perfection and comprehensiveness is more complete, He built it upon the Greatest Name, which is the last of the apparent names and the first of the hidden names. No association at all occurs in it, to repel every obstinate challenge and to indicate that whoever is not named by it does not deserve divinity. He left the sentence free of a conjunctive particle because it is like the conclusion of the first sentence and its proof. So He said, revealing to the souls of the believers and to the scholars, repeating the Name and not using a pronoun, lest it be thought restricted to a state of concealment or to something else: ﴿Allah﴾, i.e., He whose divinity and oneness are established, not other than Him. ﴿The Samad﴾, whose absolute lordship has reached its limit in everything [to a degree at which hopes fall short, so that He is such that He needs nothing] and everything is in need of Him. He is exalted above hollowness, so that nothing reaches His presence by act or by power, because He is exalted above division in every respect, together with a greatness to which no greatness is comparable. So He is one in every respect, and that is the meaning of oneness, both as expression and as indication. So He is the one to whom one turns in needs, i.e., the one intended for them. He is the one described by this Name absolutely and in every respect. Therefore He is the Creator of the world, because the world is composite by evident observation, and so it is contingent, and so its originator must be necessary and eternal, negating the two impossible things: circular dependence (*dawr*) and infinite regress (*tasalsul*). And His creation [for Him] is by power and choice, because if it were by nature and necessitation, its existence would coincide with His existence, since the cause does not separate from the effect. It would then follow that the eternity of the Creator, mighty and majestic, entails the eternity of the world, and that the origination of the world entails the origination of the Creator, majestic and exalted, and that is combining two contradictories, which is impossible. And the restriction of *samadiyya* to Him: the intensification of the alif, for the need of a thing for something other than itself, may be what causes its specific attribution to Him to be hidden. He did not restrict the oneness (*ahadiyya*), either to alert to the fact that, because of its extreme clarity, it is independent of emphasis, or to win them over, lest they flee before hearing the whole surah. And by the manifestness of the restriction of *samadiyya*, one of whose two meanings is necessarily tied to oneness, the exclusivity of oneness became evident. The scholars, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on them, said: *al-Samad* is from *samada ilayhi*, meaning when one intends him. It is like *al-Ahad*, patterned on this form because no resemblance reaches it and no similarity approaches it, for it is a special name. He is the Master to whom one turns. He is also the one who has no hollowness and no looseness in any way, because hollows are containers, and every container is in need of one who fills it. It is said: a thing is *musammad*, i.e., solid, and a stone is *samad*: smooth, not accepting dust, and nothing enters it nor comes out of it. Ibn Qutayba said: and in this sense, the *dal* in it is substituted from the *ta'*, and it means the solid (*al-musmat*). It is also the high one whose height has reached its limit. The Arabs say of what is raised from the ground: *samd*, with the *mim* vowelled with sukun, and a building that is *samad*, i.e., (p-376) elevated. So, according to the first interpretation, it is among the relational attributes, meaning that He is the master of every existent, and all are in need of Him at the beginning of their origination and in their nurture. They turn to Him in needs and intend Him in all desires, and He is absolutely independent. That is His being described by the attributes of divinity. Al-Iqlishi said: So, according to this, i.e., that He is the one who is resorted to and relied upon because His mastery has reached its limit, all the attributes of mastery branch out from the attribute of *samad*: generosity, forbearance, and other things. And if we say that *samad* means the exalted, then all the attributes of loftiness branch out from it: might, subjugation, highness, and the like. End of quotation. Al-Bayhaqi, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, narrated with his chain from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding His saying ﴿al-Samad﴾: he said, "He is the Master who is perfect in his mastery, the Noble who is perfect in his nobility, the Great who is perfect in his greatness, the Forbearing who [has] become perfect in his forbearance, the Independent who [has] become perfect in his independence, the Mighty who [has] become perfect in his might, the Knowing who has become perfect in his knowledge, the Judge who has become perfect in his judgment; and He is the one who is perfect in all kinds of nobility and mastery, and He is Allah, mighty and majestic. This is His attribute, which is not fitting except to Him, (p-377) He has no equal, and there is nothing like Him. So glory be to Allah, the One, the Subduer." Ibn Taymiyya al-Hanbali [said] in his book *al-Furqan bayna Awliya' al-Rahman wa Awliya' al-Shaytan*: The salaf of this community and its imams are agreed that the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, is distinct from His creation. He is described by what He described Himself with and by what His Messenger (ﷺ) described Him with, without distortion or negation, and without modality or likening, with an attribute of the attributes of perfection [apart from the attributes of deficiency, and we know that there is nothing like Him and no equal to Him in any of the attributes of perfection], as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1], ﴿Allah, the Samad﴾, to the end of it. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "al-Samad," to the end of what has passed from him. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: He is the one who has no hollowness, and *al-Ahad* is the one who has no equal. So His Name *al-Samad* includes His being described by the attributes of perfection and the negation of deficiencies from Him, and His Name *al-Ahad* includes that He has no like. Al-Harrali said: *al-Samad*, meaning with sukun, is the turning toward Him with needs to a Sufficient One who fulfils them, who needs no other. Therefore *al-Samad* is a master who is not mastered; the Master is Allah. End of quotation. According to the second interpretation, it is among the negative attributes. It indicates the negation of the quiddity (*mahiyya*) by which Pharaoh was obstinate, because it entails constituents, which entail need for that by which they are constituted; and it indicates the affirmation of the Essence (*huwiyya*), exalted above every trace of deficiency. For everything that has a quiddity has an inside and an interior, and that is its quiddity; and what has no interior is existent, so there is no direction and no consideration in its essence except existence. So He is the Necessary Existent, not susceptible to non-existence. It is known from this that it comprises what was mentioned before it, because this second interpretation branches out into names that look to the negation of composition, like *al-Ahad* and the like. These two interpretations, the first and the second, together encompass everything that has been explained by it. And as for what may be said of Him, glory be to Him, in terms of attributes of perfection and the descriptions of greatness and majesty: whoever is one to whom one turns in all needs, and who is exalted above every trace of created imperfection and every stain of deficiency, is the originator of everything He wills of benefit and harm, of the beneficial and the harmful, able to preserve what He wills. It is known as clearly as the sun that He has no partner, and that He alone deserves worship, because all need Him with absolute need, and His independence from them is absolute independence, and His singularity in the attributes of perfection, and His being free of any peer. And to samadiyya the turning ends, which is complete devotion. It refutes the philosophers who say that intellects govern, and the Sabians who say that stars govern, and others, [everyone who] claims governance for other than Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. Whoever believes in His samadiyya, which requires perfection of essence and attributes and the comprehensiveness of governance, (p-379) it produces in him complete reliance and trust, which is the oneness of lordship. These four names point to the stations of travellers, the aims of the bewildered and the wayward. The those brought near (*al-muqarrabun*) looked at things and found that everything other than Him, glory be to Him and exalted, is non-existent in its essence, so their remembrance was *Huwa* [and]. The people of the right looked at the existence of possible things and specified their intended object and distinguished their referent by the Majesty. The people of the left permitted plurality in the God, so they needed, in mentioning Him, to describe Him with oneness and samadiyya. These are a decisive refutation of the people of incarnation (*ittihad*) in the greatest way, for they say that the God is this world, which is divided by the senses, let alone what else, and in greater need.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah 112, verse 3:

When the explanation of His essence, glorified and exalted is He, was complete, and that He is not composite in any way at all, and when He, glorified is He, showed through His *ṣamadiyya* (the quality of being *al-Ṣamad*, the Eternal Refuge on whom all depend), which entails His oneness (*waḥdāniyya*), that everything is dependent upon Him and in need of Him, and that He is the One who gives existence to all existing things and bestows generosity upon all quiddities (*māhiyyāt*, the whatness of things), so He resembles nothing and nothing resembles Him, and there is no equal to Him in any of that. Since it may have occurred to the thought of some deluded person that for something else to be begotten from Him would be part of His perfect sovereignty, expressed by His power, He made clear that this is impossible, because it entails need, which has no connection to power, since power by its nature does not relate to the impossible. And this (p-380) is impossible, because He, glorified is He, is *Ṣamad*. Thus that [was an explanation -] of *ṣamadiyya* in both of its meanings. So He said, without a conjunction, indicating the negation of hollowness (*jawf*), which is one of the two meanings of *ṣamad*, revealing to the intelligent and explaining: nothing equals Him in a kind that could be begotten from Him, nor is there a genus from which He is born, nor anything else that could match Him in existence or otherwise: ﴿He begets not﴾, that is, it is not valid, and it is not fitting in any way whatsoever, that the begetting of another from Him should occur even once, let alone more than that. For that would entail hollowness, and He is *Ṣamad*, having no hollowness, because hollowness is a quality of the self (*nafs*), which entails need, whereas He, by His permanence in His everlastingness, is free of need of anyone who might succeed Him or assist Him, since need and annihilation are impossible for Him. So this is a refutation of those who said: the angels are the daughters of God, or 'Uzayr, or the Messiah, or others.

When he showed that He has no differentia, it became clear that He has no genus, so he pointed to it by His saying: ﴿nor is He begotten﴾. For if another were begotten from Him, He Himself would be begotten from another, as is known and rationally understood. He is eternal, having no beginning; rather He is the First, to whom non-existence never preceded. Begetting does not occur and does not take individual form except through matter and its connection, and everything that is material, or that has a connection to matter, is begotten from another. Therefore it is not valid that anything be begotten from Him, because it is not valid that He Himself be begotten from another (p-381). For He has no quiddity, and there is no consideration of His existence other than that He is He. His identity belongs to His essence, and whoever's identity belongs to his essence cannot in any way be begotten from another, for if He were begotten from another, He would not be He by His essence, and He would not be a true One or *Ṣamad*; thus it is negated from its root, and nothing would belong to Him from His essence except non-existence. It has thus become clear that He is *Wājib al-Wujūd* (the Necessary Existent). He made clear, as plainly as the sun, that He is not material, because He is not in need in any way, so it is not valid that anything be begotten from Him, since it was not valid that He be begotten from another. Whoever is like this has no like, so it is not valid in any way that anything should equal Him, so that it could stand in His place in what has been shown to be negated in the First and the Last. He indicated this, completing the explanation of His essence, which is expressed by the word "Huwa" [bi-Huwa], by His saying:

(p-382) **"And there is not to Him any equal (kufu'an)"**, that is, it is not established or found in any way, nor by any supposition, that **"anyone"** (ahad) at all is **"equal"** (kufu'an) to Him specifically, meaning a peer and one who is comparable to Him. That is, no one equals Him in the strength of existence. For if anyone were equal to Him in that, their equality would be by way of genus (jins) and differentia (fasl), so their existence would be generated from the pairing (izdiwaj) that results from a genus, which is like the mother, and a differentia, which is like the father. It has already been established that it is in no way valid for anything to be subject to begetting, because His existence is necessary through His essence. Thus nothing can equal Him in the strength of His existence, and so it is definitively negated that anyone equals Him in any part of the strength of His acts. (p-383) He conjoined these two sentences to the sentence before them, because the three together are an explanation of the "self-sufficiency" (samadiyyah) that negates the categories of likeness. They are therefore like one sentence. He placed the adverbial phrase first in the third sentence, because the greatest intended purpose is the negation of any counterpart to the Greatest Essence, so it was more important. "Kufu'an" is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "ahad."

It is also permissible for "kana" to be a defective (naqisah) verb, with "kufu'an" as its predicate. What permits its predicate status is the restriction of it by "lahu," as they have said in "in kanat lakumu al-dar al-akhirah 'inda Allah" (Qur'an 2:94). It has been made clear that this surah is the greatest clarifier of the Most Holy Essence, through an arrangement that cannot be conceived by the intellect as having anything equal to Him, and through words that cannot occur to the imagination as having anything equal to them or equal to any one of them. He first established His pure reality and His identity by saying that He is "Huwa" (He), with no name for that reality as such other than this. Thus it is known that He is necessarily existent through His essence, not through anything else at all. Then he followed this with a clarification of Him by mentioning divinity (ilahiyyah), which is the closest of the necessary attributes to that reality and the most definitive in identifying it.

Since divinity requires unity, for it is an expression for absolute self-sufficiency, and for the absolute need of everything other than Him toward Him, He indicated it by "ahad." He indicated the realization of the meaning of divinity and unity together by "al-samad," because of the two meanings it contains: necessary existence through the absence of hollowness (jawf), whether in actual existence or in supposition, and the sovereignty that bestows every existence upon every existent in a manner unlike His own existence, glory be to Him:

"Where is the Pleiades from the hand of one who would reach it?"
"The matter is greater than the saying of any speaker."

He explained both meanings by the impossibility of begetting from Him or of Him, and by the absence of any equal. So from the beginning of the surah to the end of the names, it explains His true reality, glory be to Him and exalted, and its closest necessary attributes, in order of closeness, and its unity in every respect. Then from there to its end, it explains that He has no equal, because He has no genus or species, such that He would be generated from something or something would be generated from Him, or that anything would be parallel to Him in existence. With this degree of explanation, complete knowledge of His essence is attained, and that nothing equals Him in the strength of His existence. Therefore nothing equals Him in the totality of His acts, by the evidence of the witness of existence that revealed it, and by the testimony of the victory of His Prophet (ﷺ), who used to call Abu Lahab and all the disbelievers who hated him, alone, though they filled the earth, and who informed them, despite all of them combining against him, that they would be defeated, and that he had come to them with slaughter (al-dhabh), because the one who sent him has complete encompassment of all perfection. The matter was as he (ﷺ) said, for his statements were true, so his messages were established for all creation. The content of the whole surah was established by what was established (p-384) from these well-known proofs and decisive, victorious demonstrations. It has been established that He is "al-Samad" by what indicates one of its two meanings, which is the negation of hollowness through the absence of begetting, and the other meaning, which is reaching the ultimate limit of sovereignty through the absence of any counterpart. It became clear that He is He in His essence, and there is no god other than Him. Thus the end of it coincides with its beginning, and its joints join together in the most perfect joining with what connects them. It is known that He is He and not other, with the added point that He is "al-Ahad," and there is truly no one one (ahad) apart from Him. From the realization of the end of it, one turns entirely toward Him, glory be to Him, and does not turn to anything else, because all things are in His grip.

I have quoted in my book Masa'id al-Nazar (ʿan al-Ihya') from Imam al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, on some of the secrets of this surah, a discourse that is of the utmost preciousness.

Al-Tirmidhi related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the polytheists said: O Muhammad, trace for us the lineage of your Lord. So Allah revealed: 'Say: He is Allah, One' (Qur'an 112:1), to the end of it." He said: "Because there is nothing that is born except that it will die, and nothing that dies except that it will be inherited, and Allah, exalted is He, does not die and is not inherited, and there is no one equal to Him." End of quotation. Whoever is like this is the one who encompasses all the Most Beautiful Names and the Highest Attributes, and he knows that the sum of them is the transcendence of the Worshipped One above having any homogeneous counterpart (mujanis) or any equal (mukafi'), and the refutation of everyone who opposes Him in any of that. The greatest purpose of Aal 'Imran is its debate with this surah, in refuting the end by the beginning (p-385), beginning with "al-Hayy al-Qayyum" (Qur'an 3:2), which deposits the clearest proofs against the disbelief of whoever disbelieved in Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, especially whoever claimed that 'Isa, peace be upon him, is a god, or that he is a son of Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. Likewise, it demonstrates the falsity of the doctrine of whoever claimed him to be a god, and that 'Isa, peace be upon him, is one of His servants, whom He brought into existence as He willed, just as He brought into existence one who is stranger in state than him, and it refutes whoever claimed anything else about him.

When this surah defined the reality of the Essence in the most complete definition, and the ultimate aim of seeking all the sciences is knowledge of His essence, glory be to Him and exalted, and His attributes, and the manner in which acts proceed from Him, and the Mighty Qur'an is sufficient for all these sciences, and this surah has taken on, from it, everything related to the investigation of the Essence by way of allusion and indication, and it was equivalent to a third of the Qur'an, it is also a third by another consideration, which is that religion is belief ('i'tiqad), and a verbal act that expresses belief, and an act that validates that. It suffices for the matter of belief in the Oneness (wahdaniyyah), which is the head of belief. And by the consideration that its aims are all confined to the explanation of creeds, rulings and stories, this surah, despite its brevity (p-386), has included all the divine knowledges and the refutation of whoever deviated regarding them. Because this is the primary aim, which all the other aims follow, it was equated in some sayings with the whole Qur'an. The summary of the explanation of this great surah is that He, glory be to Him and exalted, indicated the Most Holy Essence through the Identity (huwiyyah), and expressed it by the pronoun, as an indication of the negation of quiddity (mahiyyah), in which the greatest ingrate, Pharaoh, erred or deceived, may Allah's curse be upon him and upon his followers among the people of atheism, and his helpers and partisans among the people of incarnation (ittihad). He indicated this by the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam), on which there is consensus, and He indicated it by the unity that encompasses independence, which negates plurality that necessitates need. He indicated it by "al-Samad," which negates hollowness and affirms hidden sovereignty. He indicated the first of its two meanings by the negation of begetting from Him and of Him, which two indicate the negation of genus for the people and of the divisible differentia. He indicated the second by the absence of a counterpart. He indicated this absence by His great, observed acts, which the arrangement of the surahs definitively points to, by what this surah's placement in this position has led to, namely, its being brought to mind.

Reflect on what this religion's education has involved through the victory of His Prophet, whom He sent (ﷺ) to establish it. He gave power to the disbelievers, who filled the earth, over his harm, and made the greatest of them in harming him the nearest of them to him in lineage, his uncle Abu Lahab, who would follow him in those gatherings and tribes, and accompany him in those seasons, assemblies and meetings, openly declaring him a liar whenever he called the people to the truth, and confronting him with what is most hateful and most difficult to the soul. That fame became the very essence of elevation and victory (p-387), because when a thing goes beyond its limit, it turns into its opposite. For when its fame reaches its height, and then its falsehood or its truth becomes evident, its fame, by being false or true, returns greater than it would have been had no previous fame preceded it of any other kind. Thus victory was turned around, and the multitude became mighty, mutual aid was made manifest, opposition vanished, agreement was achieved, and dissension ceased. So this greatest act demonstrates the truthfulness of the Messenger (ﷺ), and that he is alone, while they who were stubborn opponents, whom none can count but Allah, lied in all that he said and all that they said. It demonstrates His might, glory be to Him and exalted, in that He gave victory to His servant in that extraordinary manner that breaks customary norms, and His wisdom in what He gave power to them over him, until fame spread swiftly and victory became general. Thus, by that witnessing, one knows that He is the Mighty, the Wise, as the surah of Tawhid (Sincerity) indicates, which corresponds to this one in refuting the end by the beginning, and which is Aal 'Imran, corresponding to this one in indicating unity and refuting whoever claimed that He has a consort and a son. It is therefore known with certainty that He has no equal, and so it is known that it is not valid at all that He begets or is begotten. Thus the claim of the divinity of 'Isa, peace be upon him, and of anyone else to whom sonship was attributed, is definitively invalidated, by the oneness that divinity requires, because begetting entails matter, which requires plurality and necessitates need. The explanation was magnified by what the Greatest Name indicates through consensus, by what divinity requires, and there is no consensus on anything other than it. The matter became exalted and the dispute ended (p-388) by what the pronoun indicates of necessary existence, which negates everything other than Him from every existent. And Allah is the Guide.

The surah has clarified, in the most excellent ways, that the one who sent him (ﷺ) is the most majestic of existents, the most noble of realities, the most precious of known things, and the greatest of essences. That necessitates the negation of everything that is not fitting, and the attainment of everything that is fitting, with a necessitation that cannot be separated, like singularity in the odd number (witr), and duality in the even number (shaf'). The detail of this is in ten matters, to be spread over the words of the surah in order:

The first: He, exalted is He, possesses existence which has no like. He is not like the contingent beings, which are preceded by non-existence, cut off by annihilation, and terminated in duration. Rather, He is eternal without beginning, everlasting without end, self-subsisting (qayyum) without cessation.

The second: He possesses subbuhiyyah (transcendence), which repels every deficiency and defect.

The third: He possesses qudusiyyah (holiness), which includes being characterized by every perfection, of majesty, beauty and exaltation.

The fourth: He possesses greatness and majesty, transcending being an accident or like accidents, or a substance or like substances, or a body or like bodies.

The fifth: He possesses loftiness, transcending indwelling in anything, or anything indwelling in Him, or uniting with anything, or anything uniting with Him.

The sixth: He, exalted is He, possesses independence from the originator, such as a Lord, and from the one who necessitates, such as a father, and from the one who bestows, that is, any of the perfections.

The seventh: He, exalted is He, possesses oneness (wahdaniyyah), in which there is no resemblance (p-389), that is, in His attributes, and no likeness, that is, in species or lineage, such as kinship.
